lfs1991.title: The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System
lfs1991.author: Mendel Rosenblum and John K. Ousterhout
lfs1991.venue: Proceedings of the 13th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '91). Camera-ready PDF, page footers dated July 24, 1991.
lfs1991.quote: a log-structured file system stores data permanently in the log: there is no other structure on disk.
additional_quotes: Even when the overhead for cleaning is included, Sprite LFS can use 70% of the disk bandwidth for writing, whereas Unix file systems typically can use only 5-10%.

For a log-structured file system to operate efficiently, it must ensure that there are always large extents of free space available for writing new data. This is the most difficult challenge in the design of a log-structured file system.

In this paper we present a solution based on large extents called segments, where a segment cleaner process continually regenerates empty segments by compressing the live data from heavily fragmented segments.
This paper will appear in the Proceedings of the 13th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles and the February 1992 ACM Transactions on Computer Systems.
The process of copying live data out of a segment is called segment cleaning.
Sprite LFS currently uses segment sizes of either 512 kilobytes or one megabyte.
Mendel Rosenblum and John K. Ousterhout / Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, Computer Science Division / University of California / Berkeley, CA 94720
In designing a log-structured file system we decided to focus on the efficiency of small-file accesses, and leave it to hardware designers to improve bandwidth for large-file accesses.

The notion of logging is not new, and a number of recent file systems have incorporated a log as an auxiliary structure to speed up writes and crash recovery[2, 3]. However, these other systems use the log only for temporary storage; the permanent home for information is in a traditional random-access storage structure on disk.
supports: the log is the only on-disk structure, not a recovery aid
70% of disk bandwidth for writing against 5-10% for Unix file systems
free space is the hardest problem in the design
SOSP '91 venue, and the February 1992 TOCS reprint
Sprite LFS was aimed at small-file office and engineering workloads, not transaction processing
some, not all, contemporary file systems kept a log, and only as an auxiliary structure

lfstocs1992.title: The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System (ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 10(1), February 1992, pages 26-52)
lfstocs1992.author: Mendel Rosenblum and John K. Ousterhout
lfstocs1992.venue: ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, Vol. 10, No. 1, February 1992, Pages 26-52
lfstocs1992.quote: These write cost figures imply that the cleaning overhead limits the long-term write performance to about 70% of the maximum sequential write bandwidth.
additional_quotes: The log is the only structure on disk; it contains indexing information so that files can be read back from the log efficiently.
Even when the overhead for cleaning is included, Sprite LFS can use 70% of the disk bandwidth for writing, whereas Unix file systems typically can use only 5 - 10%.
Even though the overall disk capacity utilizations ranged from 11 - 75%, more than half of the segments cleaned were totally empty.
supports: the 70% figure is measured on production Sprite LFS file systems, not only simulated

seltzer1995.title: File System Logging Versus Clustering: A Performance Comparison
seltzer1995.author: Margo Seltzer, Keith A. Smith, Hari Balakrishnan, Jacqueline Chang, Sara McMains, Venkata Padmanabhan
seltzer1995.venue: USENIX 1995 Technical Conference, New Orleans, LA, January 1995 — the venue is not on the PDF's front matter; the paper's own reference [2] names it, and Ousterhout's critique calls it "the Winter 1995 USENIX Conference".
seltzer1995.quote: The good news is that this performance is comparable to FFS, but the unfortunate result is that any performance advantage of LFS is already lost at a file system utilization of only 48%.
additional_quotes: In the absence of the cleaner, LFS provides approximately 50% better performance than FFS.

The introduction of the cleaner changes the results substantially. At a file system utilization of 48%, LFS performance is comparable to FFS, yielding a performance degradation of 34% due to the cleaner.
We examine LFS cleaner performance in a transaction processing environment and find that cleaner overhead reduces LFS performance by more than 33% when the disk is 50% full.
Cleaning overhead can degrade LFS performance by more than 34% in a transaction processing environment.
The TPC-B benchmark simulates a check-cashing application [13].
Margo Seltzer, Keith A. Smith / Harvard University / Hari Balakrishnan, Jacqueline Chang, Sara McMains, Venkata Padmanabhan / University of California, Berkeley
Figure 7. Transaction processing performance. While LFS can potentially provide dramatically improved performance, when the cleaner runs, its performance is comparable to FFS.
supports: without the cleaner LFS beat FFS by approximately 50%
with the cleaner, at 48% utilization, a 34% degradation and the advantage gone
the workload was TPC-B on 4.4BSD-LFS against the 4.4BSD Fast File System

oustercritique.title: A Critique of Seltzer's LFS Measurements
oustercritique.author: John Ousterhout
oustercritique.quote: Thus, of the three main results sections (Sections 3, 4, and 5) only the results in Section 3 are completely reliable;  the others should be taken with a grain of salt.
additional_quotes: The paper "File System Logging Versus Clustering: A Performance Comparison", by Margo Seltzer et al., appears in the Winter 1995 USENIX Conference.

The measurements in Section 4 are counter-intuitive, and the back-of-the-envelope calculations used to support those measurements are incorrect. At present neither Seltzer nor I can explain the measurements.
supports: Ousterhout published a public critique of the measurements

seltzerresponse.title: A Response to Ousterhout's Critique of LFS Measurements
seltzerresponse.author: Margo Seltzer et al.
seltzerresponse.quote: John Ousterhout has posted a web page questioning measurements in the 1995 Usenix paper Logging versus Clustering: A Performance Evaluation. This page responds to the issues raised by Ousterhout.
additional_quotes: To date, we are aware of no technical inaccuracies in the paper.
The simulated results presented in Figure 4 of the TOCS paper are for the greedy cleaning algorithm.  This is not the cleaning algorithm implemented in either Sprite-LFS or BSD-LFS
supports: Seltzer published a response; each page disputes the other's reading and neither concedes

lsmtree1996.title: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)
lsmtree1996.author: Patrick O'Neil, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick, Elizabeth O'Neil
lsmtree1996.venue: Acta Informatica 33(4), June 1996, pages 351-385 (Crossref/publisher metadata). The PDF read is the preprint, headed "To be published: Acta Informatica".
lsmtree1996.quote: The idea of always writing multi-page blocks to new locations was inspired by the Log-Structured File System devised by Rosenblum and Ousterhout [23], from which the Log-Structured Merge-tree takes its name.
additional_quotes: In the Log-Structured File System, the reuse of old blocks involves significant I/O because blocks are typically only partially freed up, so reuse requires a block read and block write. In the LSM-Tree, blocks are totally freed up on the trailing edge of the rolling merge, so no extra I/O is involved.
supports: LSM trees take their name and their write-to-new-locations idea from LFS
the LSM authors name LFS's reclamation cost as the thing they route around

unverified: The publication dates of the two web pages in the exchange. Neither 'A Critique of Seltzer's LFS Measurements' nor 'A Response to Ousterhout's Critique of LFS Measurements' carries a date; both are dated 1995 here from the paper they argue about. The archived critique gives Ousterhout's address as john.ousterhout@scriptics.com, and Scriptics postdates 1995, so the copy that survives was revised after the exchange.
That the argument was never formally settled. Both pages exist and neither concedes, but no source read here says the question was closed.
Whether Sprite LFS or BSD-LFS was ever the default file system of a shipped release, and what happened to BSD-LFS maintenance afterwards.
Any dollar figure. None of the sources price the outcome; the cost was the design losing the workload it was aimed at.
Keith Bostic's role. He co-authored the 1993 BSD-LFS paper cited as [10] by Seltzer 1995, but that paper was not opened here, so he is not named in the story.

Whether cleaning ever got cheaper after 1995. Later work attacks exactly that — Seltzer 1995's own reference [2] is "Heuristic Cleaning Algorithms in LFS" — and no source read here settles it, so the story claims only that a log-structured store must pay for its own reclamation, not that the price never fell.
